extracted.intended_audience: power plant owners/operators, state and federal regulators, EPA rule commenters, and other stakeholders involved in CAA section 111 rulemaking for electric generating units (EGUs)
extracted.subtask_description: Guidance and rationale used by EPA to determine the Best System of Emission Reduction (BSER) for fossil fuel-fired electric generating units, including assessment of CCS, natural gas co-firing, efficiency measures, and the policy/economic context that affects feasibility and cost-reasonableness.

rubrics_metrics.name: Carbon Capture and Storage (CCS) technology readiness and deployment timing
rubrics_metrics.description: EPA reviewed current state and cost of CCS technology for use with both steam generating units and stationary combustion turbines; multiple projects are in advanced stages and/or have completed FEED studies, and several projects (e.g., Linde/BASF pilot at Dallman, NET Power Allam-Fetvedt cycle) demonstrate pilot/early-commercial performance and indicate potential to commence operation well before January 1, 2032.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use evidence from small-scale pilot studies, FEED studies, techno-economic analyses, and project announcements to assess whether CCS is sufficiently mature and can be built and commence operation within relevant timeframes. Examples cited: Linde/BASF 10 MW pilot and NET Power 300 MW Allam-Fetvedt project (designed >97% capture). See accompanying RIA and final TSDs in docket for detailed evaluation.

rubrics_metrics.name: CCS cost reasonableness and capital amortization constraint
rubrics_metrics.description: While CCS promises significant emissions reductions, it requires substantial up-front capital expenditure and therefore is not feasible or cost-reasonable for units that intend to cease operation before they would be able to amortize its costs.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When determining which units the BSER should apply to, avoid imposing costly control obligations on coal-fired plants that have announced voluntary retirement; assess whether owners/operators can feasibly and cost-effectively deploy CCS given anticipated remaining operating life and amortization horizon.

rubrics_metrics.name: Natural gas co-firing technical capability and required modifications
rubrics_metrics.description: Natural gas co-firing is the substitution of natural gas for some coal so a unit fires a combination of coal and natural gas. Existing coal-fired steam generating units can be modified to co-fire in any desired proportion; modification generally involves installation of new gas burners, related boiler modifications, and potentially construction of a natural gas supply pipeline if none exists.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Evaluate on-site multi-fuel capability, burner modifications, pipeline capacity and sizing, and historical hourly co-firing rates (e.g., 249 of 565 units reported use of natural gas; 29 units co-fired ≥60% on an hourly basis). Consider documented conversions and past experience (over 80 utility boilers converted to gas since 2011) as evidence of technical feasibility.

rubrics_metrics.name: Natural gas co-firing cost and market drivers
rubrics_metrics.description: The cost of natural gas co-firing has declined because the expected difference between coal and gas prices has decreased and analysis supports lower capital costs for modifying existing boilers to co-fire with natural gas.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Consider fuel price differentials, capital cost estimates for boiler modifications, and relevant analyses (see section VII.C.2.a and RIA/TSD) when assessing cost-reasonableness and practical deployment of co-firing as a BSER measure.

rubrics_metrics.name: Efficient generation for combustion turbines (BSER for certain new/reconstructed turbines)
rubrics_metrics.description: Highly efficient generation is the BSER technology upon which the first phase standards of performance are based for certain new and reconstructed stationary combustion turbine EGUs; applicable to both simple cycle and combined cycle turbines and demonstrated—along with best O&M practices—to reduce emissions.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Assess thermal efficiency improvements (e.g., increased firing temperature, higher pressure ratios, intercooling, inlet air cooling) and best operating/maintenance practices (proper maintenance of flow path components, HRSG pairing, insulation, blowdown heat recovery, minimizing steam leaks, minimizing air infiltration, cleaning heat transfer surfaces). Recognize these improvements are often incremental, achieved by many recently constructed turbines, and present relatively little incremental capital or compliance cost compared to other technologies.

rubrics_metrics.name: Efficiency improvements for steam generating units—magnitude and limitations
rubrics_metrics.description: Efficiency improvements for steam generating EGUs include technology upgrades and operating practices that may achieve CO2 emission rate reductions of approximately 0.1 to 5 percent for individual EGUs, which are small relative to reductions achievable from natural gas co-firing and CCS.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Account for modest relative CO2 reductions and potential for the 'rebound effect' (efficiency-induced increased utilization leading to greater aggregate emissions). Because of small overall GHG reductions and potential perverse outcomes, EPA did not finalize efficiency improvements as the BSER for any subcategory of existing coal-fired steam generating units. See final TSD and HRI report for specifics on measures, costs, and limitations.

rubrics_metrics.name: BSER scope principle—focus on measures that improve individual-source pollution performance
rubrics_metrics.description: In determining the CAA section 111 emission limitations included in these final actions, EPA focused on 'measures that improve the pollution performance of individual sources,' not generation technologies that entities could employ as alternatives to fossil fuel-fired EGUs.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When evaluating candidate BSER measures, prioritize technologies and practices that directly reduce emissions at the subject source (e.g., CCS retrofits, combustion turbine efficiency improvements, co-firing) rather than system-level generation changes (e.g., replacing a coal plant with renewables) that are alternatives to the source itself.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use of evidence and documentation to justify BSER (FEED, pilots, RIA, TSD)
rubrics_metrics.description: EPA's determination relied on review of FEED studies, pilot projects, techno-economic analyses, and the accompanying Regulatory Impact Analysis (RIA) and final Technical Support Documents (TSDs), which are included in the rulemaking docket.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Substantiate claims of feasibility, cost, and performance with FEED studies, pilot/demonstration project results, techno-economic analysis, and the RIA/TSD. Cite specific docket materials when using such evidence in BSER justification.

rubrics_metrics.name: IRA/IIJA incentives and tax-credit eligibility criteria affecting CCUS deployment (IRC section 45Q)
rubrics_metrics.description: IRA increased tax credit incentives for capturing and storing CO2; for the power sector, a qualifying carbon capture facility must have a CO2 capture design capacity of not less than 75 percent of the baseline CO2 production of the unit and construction must begin before January 1, 2033. The increased credit values are $85/metric ton for CO2 captured and securely stored and $60/metric ton for CO2 captured and utilized or incidentally stored for EOR, with credits claimable for 12 years.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Consider enhanced tax credits and eligibility deadlines in assessing the economic feasibility of CCUS deployment. Note provisions for direct payment to certain tax-exempt entities, 5-year direct payment election for tax-paying entities, and the ability to transfer credits to unrelated taxpayers in some circumstances — these provisions materially affect project finance and deployment prospects.

rubrics_metrics.name: Clean hydrogen production tax credit tiers (IRC section 45V)
rubrics_metrics.description: Section 45V codifies production tax credits for 'clean hydrogen' with tiered credit values based on estimated GHG emissions of the hydrogen production process; e.g., $3/kg H2 for <0.45 kg CO2e/kg H2 down to $0.6/kg H2 for 2.5–4.0 kg CO2e/kg H2; projects with >4.0 kg CO2e/kg H2 are not eligible.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When assessing potential low-GHG hydrogen pathways connected to EGUs or CCUS, use the 45V emission thresholds and tiered credit values (and any wage/apprenticeship prerequisites) to estimate project economics and influence on BSER feasibility/options.

rubrics_metrics.name: Consideration of power sector trends and market dynamics
rubrics_metrics.description: EPA considered long-term sectoral trends (decline of coal generation, growth of natural gas and renewables, aging coal fleet, retirements, capacity additions in gas/solar/wind/storage, and changing fuel prices) when determining which controls qualify as BSER and where they can be feasibly deployed.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: In BSER analysis, factor in historical and projected generation mixes, retirement schedules, fuel price trajectories, and the pace of new clean generation and storage deployment (EIA and other model projections cited). These trends affect both the opportunity and prudence of imposing particular control obligations on specific units.

rubrics_metrics.name: State laws, utility commitments, and regional programs as contextual constraints/opportunities
rubrics_metrics.description: State statutory targets, RPS/CES programs, regional markets (e.g., RGGI), and utility IRPs and announced utility commitments to emissions reductions were reviewed and recognized as influencing where and how BSER technologies (including CCS) can be deployed; examples include California SB 100 and SB 905, Montana's 50% capture requirement for certain transactions, and various state tax incentives for CCS.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Evaluate state regulatory requirements, incentive programs, and utility IRPs as part of the feasibility and cost-reasonableness assessment for BSER deployment. State-specific mandates or incentives can accelerate deployment or constrain certain uses (e.g., CARB preventing EOR use of captured CO2).

rubrics_metrics.name: Evidence of technology-specific performance and cost-reduction potential
rubrics_metrics.description: EPA cites specific project-level examples and analyses demonstrating performance and potential cost reductions (e.g., NET Power's design to achieve >97% CO2 capture; Linde/BASF 10 MW pilot and techno-economic analysis indicating significant capital cost reductions compared to NETL base case).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use concrete project data (pilot metrics, capture percentages, cost comparisons to reference cases) when judging which technologies meet BSER criteria for performance and cost-effectiveness. Documented high-capture designs and process improvements strengthen a technology's case as BSER-eligible.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoiding perverse outcomes (rebound effect) when evaluating efficiency measures
rubrics_metrics.description: As efficiency increases, some facilities could increase utilization and therefore increase their CO2 emissions (as well as emissions of other air pollutants); this phenomenon is known as the 'rebound effect' and can produce perverse GHG outcomes.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When considering efficiency measures as potential BSER actions, analyze system- and facility-level behavioral responses (e.g., increased utilization) to ensure that adopted measures produce net emissions reductions rather than offsetting gains through higher output. This consideration supported EPA's decision not to finalize efficiency improvements as BSER for existing coal-fired subcategories.
